item.title: UBS: Artisan Partners Calls on the Bank to Leave Switzerland
item.description: Artisan Partners asks UBS to leave Switzerland. The two funds manage more than 60 million shares of Switzerland's largest bank.
item.content:encoded:
## At a Glance - Artisan Partners is calling on UBS to leave Switzerland - The two funds manage over 60 million UBS shares - UBS’s CET1 capital would rise from $56 billion to $72 billion - The National Council will now review the proposal
## Key Facts - Entity → Artisan Partners - Managed stake → over 60 million UBS shares - Share of capital → over 1.8% - Calculated CET1 capital → from $56 billion to $72 billion - Market value lost → $36 billion, approximately 23% - Coverage of foreign subsidiaries → 45% today, 90% by the cantons, 100% by the Federal Council
## Artisan Partners’ Request
Over 60 million UBS shares are at the center of the letter in which Artisan Partners asked Switzerland’s largest bank to leave the country. The Global Value and International Value teams manage these shares on behalf of their clients: the stake exceeds 1.8% of UBS’s share capital.
The news was reported by Keystone-ATS. The request, attributed to the U.S. asset manager, is part of the debate over a possible relocation of the bank outside Switzerland. According to Artisan, stricter capital adequacy requirements make Switzerland no longer an attractive location for the major bank.
In the letter published today and addressed to the Board of Directors, the fund managers describe the proposed requirements as “excessive, punitive, and unnecessary.” Their calculations indicate that UBS would need to increase its CET1 capital from $56 billion to $72 billion. The fund argues that the additional $16 billion could generate returns in a country with less stringent regulations. Artisan also estimates the loss in market value at $36 billion, approximately 23% of UBS’s current market value.
### The Bank’s Response and Parliamentary Review
In the document, Artisan calls on the Board of Directors to separate from Switzerland and from a regulatory system that, according to the fund managers, leaves no real choice. UBS has acknowledged receipt of the open letter. A spokesperson, when asked by AWP, reiterated that the goal is to continue operating successfully as a global bank from Switzerland.
The bank added that it will protect shareholders’ interests and provide data and analysis to support an informed decision. UBS supports targeted, proportionate, and internationally coordinated regulation capable of addressing the causes of the Credit Suisse crisis.
On the institutional front, the Federal Council wants 100% coverage for holdings in foreign subsidiaries with hard core capital. Last week, the Council of States opted for 90%; currently, the requirement stands at 45%. The bill now goes to the National Council. UBS also considers the stricter version proposed by the Council of States to be excessive and estimates that this solution would require approximately $16 billion in additional capital. ## What the Three Thresholds Mean
The comparison lists three numbers, but does not treat them as equal. 45% is the current target; 90% is the figure chosen by the Council of States, the Chamber of the Cantons; 100% is the Federal Council’s target. The bill now moves to the National Council. For those who follow Swiss economic policy, this step prevents treating either of the two proposed thresholds as a foregone conclusion.
| Reference | Threshold | Source | | Current situation | 45% | Currently indicated threshold | | Council of States | 90% | Slightly less stringent option | | Federal Council | 100% | Required coverage for investments in foreign subsidiaries |
### Capital Amount and Location
The same caution applies to the $16 billion. Artisan links this figure to the increase in CET1 from 56 to 72 billion and argues that this amount could generate returns in a country with less stringent regulations. UBS, on the other hand, estimates an additional capital requirement of approximately 16 billion under the Council of States’ proposal. The figure matches, but the source attributes it to two different scenarios: it is not presented as an outcome already decided by the legislature.
For those living or working in Switzerland, the key point is therefore to distinguish between a request from an asset manager, a decision by the bank, and an institutional shift. Artisan considers Switzerland no longer an attractive location; UBS states that it intends to continue operating from Switzerland. A potential relocation remains described as a possibility at the center of the debate, not as a foregone conclusion.
The source takes the reader to the corporate and regulatory level. It does not outline a new procedure for clients, but illustrates how the choice of location is linked to capital requirements, the capital of foreign subsidiaries, and the international coordination required by UBS. Those who wish to keep the regulatory issues separate from their banking decisions can consult the conti bancari in Svizzera.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the net salary calculator and the CHF-EUR exchange comparator. ## How to Follow the Story
A useful approach for anyone who wants to understand the developments without reading more into the source than it actually says is to follow a four-step process.
### Four Practical Steps
1. Establish the baseline. Note that the figure indicated as the current rate is 45%. This is the starting point for comparison, not a newly approved threshold.
2. Assign each proposal. Next to 100%, indicate the Federal Council; next to 90%, indicate the Council of States. The source notes that the bill now moves to the National Council, so the two percentages should be kept as separate positions.
3. Separate the estimates. Artisan’s 16 billion is linked to the difference between 56 and 72 billion in CET1 capital. UBS’s approximately 16 billion, on the other hand, represents the estimated additional requirement under the Council of States’ solution. Always read the figure in conjunction with the entity providing it to avoid confusing the manager’s assessment with that of the bank.
4. Follow the institutional process. Artisan’s letter, UBS’s response, and the National Council’s review are three distinct elements of the dossier. The source does not report the final outcome of the project, though it already records the bank’s position on remaining in Switzerland.
This sequence is particularly useful for shareholders and clients who wish to evaluate the available information. UBS states that it will protect shareholders’ interests and continue to provide data and analysis to support well-informed decision-making. The potential exit from Switzerland, however, remains a request made by Artisan within an ongoing debate.
For a separate analysis of the daily relationship with the banking system, the comparison using conti bancari in Svizzera is available. For a distinct personal assessment, use calcolatore stipendio/imposte.

item.title: Daycare and Childcare in Valais: Costs
item.description: In Valais, daycare centers, family daycare, and after-school programs: fees are based on income, and cantonal subsidies are available for child care.
item.content:encoded:
## At a Glance - Three childcare services are listed in Valais. - Fees are calculated based on income. - Cantonal subsidies are available.
## Key Facts - Area → Canton of Valais - Services → daycare centers, family daycare providers, after-school programs - Cost criterion → income - Support → cantonal subsidies
In the Canton of Valais, the issue of child care costs revolves around three solutions: daycare centers, family daycare providers, and after-school programs. The table presents them together because families’ concerns extend beyond the mere availability of a service to include how rates are determined.
### Income Is the Key Criteria
The rule for Valais is clear: fees are calculated based on income. Therefore, there is no single flat rate applied indiscriminately to those seeking a daycare center, a family daycare provider, or an after-school program. The first factor to focus on when comparing options is the income used to calculate the fee.
In addition to the income-based fee, the table lists available cantonal subsidies. However, this support should not be treated as a standard amount or an identical reduction for everyone: the availability of subsidies must be assessed based on the specific situation. When evaluating costs, it is therefore essential to distinguish between two elements: the service fee and any cantonal support.
For those living in the Canton of Valais, this approach shifts the focus from a simple question about price to a more detailed assessment. It is necessary to identify the type of childcare, inquire how the income criterion is applied, and determine which cantonal procedure allows for verifying the subsidy. The three options remain the starting point, while income and cantonal support are the two economic factors that must be considered together.
The asilo nido guide can be used as an initial reference to organize the comparison, without confusing the availability of a subsidy with a predetermined amount. The cost of childcare should be viewed as a line item in the family budget, but without mixing it with other components of the cost of living in Switzerland. The service fee and the cantonal subsidy are part of the childcare cost comparison; premiums, contributions, and taxes, on the other hand, follow separate mechanisms.
### A Guide to Understanding the Expenses
| Item | Criteria to Apply | |---|---| | Child Care | Fee calculated based on income | | Support | Available cantonal subsidies | | LAMal/KVG | mandatory insurance for residents, with per-capita premiums; not a tax or an employer contribution | | AVS/AHV and LPP/BVG | social security and contributions separate from the childcare fee | | Taxes | direct federal tax, cantonal and municipal taxes; separate VAT |
The table separates items that affect the budget but do not serve the same function. LAMal/KVG pertains to mandatory health insurance for residents and has per-capita premiums; it is not the same as a daycare fee. AVS/AHV and LPP/BVG fall under pension and social security contributions. The Swiss tax system operates on three levels, while VAT is a separate item within the tax framework.
The reference to cantonal subsidies places this assessment at the cantonal level. For those evaluating costo della vita in Svizzera, the distinction is practical: first, the childcare arrangement and the income-based rate are examined; then, cantonal subsidies are verified; finally, other expenses—which follow their own rules—are kept separate.
In a hypothetical scenario, the most transparent comparison involves creating three columns: selected service, income-based rate, and cantonal subsidy to be verified. Only after this separation does it make sense to include other Swiss expenses alongside them. The method does not produce an automatic figure, but it clarifies what needs to be checked before making a choice.
Since the table does not indicate a standard rate, it is not advisable to replace the income criterion with a generic price. The useful data is that linked to the chosen service, the income in question, and the verification of cantonal support.

To turn this overview into a practical decision, the evaluation can follow a brief process. The goal is not to estimate a theoretical price, but to compare information gathered using the same criteria.
### Four Steps Before Making a Choice
1. Define the option to be compared. Specify whether the search concerns a daycare center, a foster family, or an after-school program. These three categories constitute the scope of the comparison in the Canton of Valais. 2. Inquire about the fee calculation method. The key question is how the cost is calculated based on income. Note the specific income figure used, so as not to compare a rate based on a different criterion. 3. Verify cantonal subsidies. After identifying the service, inquire at the cantonal level about which subsidies are available for childcare. Do not assign a standard amount to the subsidy before verifying the details. 4. Separate budget items. Keep the childcare portion distinct from other Swiss expenses, including premiums, contributions, and taxes. The final comparison must show the fee and support separately.
This sequence of steps is useful because it prevents you from starting with an isolated figure. First, determine the subject; then the economic criterion; next, the subsidy; and finally, the overall budget. If the reference income changes, the fee calculation is the item that needs to be rechecked; there is no need to replace it with an average amount unrelated to the situation at hand.
For Valais, no fixed amounts or operational deadlines are specified in the table. It is therefore correct to work with a comparison sheet and leave the fields that must be verified at the cantonal level blank, rather than filling them with generic numbers. item.title: Flight suspension in Kägiswil until 20 nov 2026
item.description: UFAC has ordered the suspension of flights from 9 October 2026 at least until 20 November 2026 at Kägiswil airfield, pending the PSIA-Rega public filing from 15 October to 16 November 2026.
item.content:encoded:
## At a Glance - Kägiswil suspends flights until at least November 20, 2026 - The FOCA has ordered the closure of the airfield - The public notice period begins on October 15, 2026 - The public notice period ends on November 16, 2026
## Key Facts - Publication → September 30, 2026 - FOCA decision → July 13, 2026 - Suspension → from October 9, 2026, until at least November 20, 2026 - Location → Kägiswil Airfield, Municipality of Sarnen (OW) - Cooperative → Obwalden Airfield Cooperative (FGOW) - Project → Rega civil heliport - Documents → PSIA and Rega’s application - Filing deadline → November 16, 2026
The federal government’s press release, published on September 30, 2026, announces the suspension of flight operations at the Kägiswil Airfield. The FOCA ordered the closure because the requirements for continuing operations are no longer met. The measure will remain in effect at least until November 20, 2026.
The decision stems from the FOCA’s denial of a building permit on July 13, 2026, as part of the change-of-use procedure. The Obwalden Airfield Cooperative (FGOW) has filed an appeal with the Federal Administrative Court. The proceedings are pending, and the change of use for civilian purposes has not yet become final.
### Why the Runway Is Being Shut Down
The surface rights agreement with armasuisse, which allows FGOW to use the airfield and hangars, expires at the end of September 2026 and has not yet been extended. Federal authorities have offered the cooperative the opportunity to negotiate a temporary continuation of operations. However, after determining that the requirements are no longer being met, the Federal Office of Civil Aviation (FOCA) has ordered the closure.
Prior to October 9, only flights intended for relocation to another location are authorized. From October 9, 2026, and at least until November 20, 2026, all flight operations must be suspended for safety reasons. During that period, Rega will need to install the necessary infrastructure in preparation for the planned new construction near the runway.
Plans for the site’s future are proceeding in parallel. Rega has submitted an application to the FOCA to establish operations at the former military airport in Kägiswil, in the municipality of Sarnen (OW). A civilian heliport is planned to replace operations with fixed-wing aircraft. The project includes a hangar building, five helicopter parking pads, and a multi-story administrative complex with an underground garage.
The public review period for the PSIA documents and Rega’s application will begin on October 15, 2026, and last for 30 days, ending on November 16, 2026. The Confederation will then evaluate the comments received and determine the next steps in the process. Regarding general mobility, the press release does not announce any changes to the mezzi pubblici regulations. A practical reading of the dossier requires distinguishing between the operation of the airfield and the proposed heliport project. The former concerns the current use of the runway; the latter requires amendments to the PSIA and an assessment by the Confederation.
### A Project Still Pending Evaluation
Public submission does not equate to a green light. The FOCA is submitting the proposed amendments to the PSIA and Rega’s application to the public; after consulting with the authorities and reviewing the comments received, the federal government will conduct a comprehensive assessment of the interests involved regarding Kägiswil Airport. Only then will it determine how to proceed. The consultation period opening on October 15, 2026, is therefore an opportunity for public participation, not an announcement of the heliport’s approval.
The FGOW appeal also leaves open the question of the originally planned change of use for civilian purposes. The Rega project is based on a different configuration than that of current operations with fixed-wing aircraft: it envisions a civilian heliport intended for technical and work flights during business hours. The source rules out a Rega operational base. Instead, it refers to the technical maintenance of the helicopter fleet and the new headquarters. For Rotex Helicopter AG, based in the region, the possibility of a base for work flights is envisaged in the long term.
### Two Time Horizons
Rega’s timeline includes a separate deadline: following the planned construction of taxiways to bypass the runway, Rega must vacate its headquarters at Zurich Airport by the end of 2030. This date pertains to the relocation of the headquarters and does not, by itself, determine when Kägiswil will be able to operate as a heliport. The press release provides no data on jobs, salaries, costs, or economic impacts; therefore, it does not allow the project to be linked to new annunci di lavoro.
For the public, the practical implication is to distinguish between what has already been decided regarding operations and what remains to be defined in terms of infrastructure. The suspension of operations and the PSIA consultation are related steps, but they are not the same: the former addresses the requirements for the use of the airfield, while the latter concerns the future civil use of the site. Whether operations will continue after November 20, 2026, also remains under negotiation, with no outcome indicated in the source.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the pension planner and the pillar 3 simulator. To follow the case without getting the deadlines mixed up, it is best to organize your attention in a specific sequence. The procedure described by the Confederation provides a public access point, while the airfield’s operations follow a separate schedule.
### Steps for Review
1. Starting October 15, 2026, review the PSIA documentation and the application submitted by Rega at the Sarnen municipal administration office. The PSIA-related documents are also available on the participation page indicated by the FOCA. 2. During the 30-day public review period, review the SIAP amendments and Rega’s construction project separately. The former concerns the aviation planning framework; the latter describes the building with a hangar, the five helicopter parking pads, and the administrative complex with an underground garage. The application calls for technical and operational flights during business hours. 3. Set November 16, 2026, as the deadline for the public consultation. Anyone wishing to submit a statement must do so within the consultation period; the Confederation will then evaluate the statements received and the consultation with the authorities. 4. After the submission period closes, monitor the outcome of the comprehensive assessment of interests and the next steps in the procedure. The source does not anticipate either the outcome or an authorization date.
### Steps Toward Operationalization
Those currently using Kägiswil must distinguish between temporary authorizations and safety suspensions. Prior to October 9, 2026, only flights intended for transfer to another location remain authorized. From October 9, 2026, until at least November 20, 2026, all flight operations must be suspended. After that date, any continuation will depend on negotiations between the Confederation and FGOW.
FGOW’s appeal before the Federal Administrative Court remains pending, while armasuisse’s lease agreement expires at the end of September 2026 and has not yet been extended. For long-term planning, the target date is the end of 2030: by then, Rega must vacate its headquarters at Zurich Airport. The source does not contain data on salaries or taxes; for a personal economic comparison, refer to calcolatore stipendio.
